source.text: Śikṣānanda, trans. (attributed), Sutra of the Original Vows of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva (Taishō T412): selections from chapters 1, 2, 6, 7 and 13 of its 13 chapters

jj01.heading: The Assembly in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven
jj01.plain: Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha was in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, teaching the Dharma for his mother. Then unspeakably many Buddhas and great bodhisattvas from the measureless worlds of the ten directions all gathered, praising Śākyamuni Buddha for showing inconceivable great wisdom and spiritual power in this evil world full of the five turbidities, taming stubborn and unruly beings so they come to know the principles of suffering and joy. Each sent attendants to pay respects to the World-Honored One.
jj01.commentary: The Kṣitigarbha Sutra was taught by the Buddha after he rose to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven for his late mother, Queen Māyā. So it has long been called "the filial-piety sutra of Buddhism" and is often read at ceremonies for departed parents and ancestors.

jj02.heading: The Elder's Son Asks the Buddha
jj02.plain: Unspeakably long ago, Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva was the son of a great elder. At that time there was a Buddha named Lion's Swift Complete Myriad Practices Tathāgata. Seeing that Buddha's holy form adorned with a thousand blessings, the elder's son asked: "What practices and vows did you make to gain such a form?" The Buddha answered: "If you wish to gain such a body, you must save all suffering beings for a very long time."
jj02.commentary: This is how Kṣitigarbha first came to make his vow. The answer is that the way to a Buddha's form is no secret technique, only saving beings who suffer.

jj03.heading: Kṣitigarbha's Great Vow
jj03.plain: Mañjuśrī, the elder's son then made a vow: "From now on, to the end of the future, for incalculable kalpas, I will use every skillful means for the beings of the six realms caught in wrongdoing and suffering, and only after liberating them all will I myself become a Buddha." Because he made this great vow before that Buddha, even now, after hundreds of thousands of millions of nayutas of unspeakable kalpas, he remains a bodhisattva.
jj03.commentary: The heart of Kṣitigarbha's vow: he will not become a Buddha until all beings are saved. It is often summed up as "Until the hells are empty, I vow not to become a Buddha." That is why Kṣitigarbha is called the Bodhisattva of the Great Vow.

jj04.heading: The Brahmin's Daughter and Her Mother
jj04.plain: And incalculable asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago there was a Buddha named Flower of Awakening, Samādhi, Sovereign King Tathāgata. … In the age when only the outward form of his teaching remained, there was a brahmin's daughter. Her merit from past lives was deep, so everyone looked up to her, and heaven protected her whether she walked, stood, sat or lay down. But her mother believed in false things and always scorned the Three Jewels. The daughter tried every way to persuade her mother to take up right views, but before her mother could fully believe, her life soon ended and she fell into the Avīci hell.
jj04.commentary: Another of Kṣitigarbha's past lives. When a beloved mother departs without ever accepting the right path, what can the child left behind do? This question runs through the whole sutra.

jj05.heading: Offerings and a Vow for Her Mother
jj05.plain: The brahmin's daughter … sold her house, gathered incense, flowers and all kinds of offerings, and made great offerings at the stupas and temples of that ancient Buddha. … Learning that through this merit her mother had left the hells and been born in heaven, the daughter returned as if waking from a dream, and before the stupa and image of Flower of Awakening, Samādhi, Sovereign King Tathāgata she made a great vow: "To the end of the future, I will use every skillful means for all beings caught in wrongdoing and suffering and bring them to liberation."
jj05.commentary: In the omitted passage, after intense prayer the daughter sees the hells, and a ghost king there tells her that thanks to her merit her mother was born in heaven three days before. It is the moment when devotion to one's own mother widens into a vow for all beings. This story is the basis of ceremonies that make merit for the departed.

jj06.heading: The Buddha's Entrustment
jj06.plain: "Kṣitigarbha, see how over many kalpas I have labored to save beings caught in wrongdoing and suffering, so hard to teach and so stubborn. Those not yet tamed receive results according to the karma they have made. When they fall into evil paths and suffer greatly, remember what I earnestly asked of you in the Trāyastriṃśa palace: liberate all the beings of this Sahā world until Maitreya Buddha comes, so that they leave all suffering forever, meet the Buddhas and receive their predictions."
jj06.commentary: From Śākyamuni Buddha's passing until Maitreya Buddha comes, the beings of this long age without a Buddha are entrusted to Kṣitigarbha. So Kṣitigarbha is the bodhisattva who looks after us in this very age.

jj07.heading: Do Not Worry
jj07.plain: Then Kṣitigarbha's bodies, divided among many worlds, became one again, and weeping in sorrow he said to the Buddha: "Since long ago I have received the Buddha's guidance and gained inconceivable spiritual power and great wisdom. My divided bodies fill worlds as many as hundreds of thousands of millions of Ganges sands; in each world I appear in hundreds of thousands of millions of bodies, and each body saves hundreds of thousands of millions of people, leading them to take refuge in the Three Jewels, leave birth and death forever and reach the joy of nirvana. … I pray, World-Honored One, do not worry about the beings of later ages who do evil." Three times he said to the Buddha: "I pray, World-Honored One, do not worry about the beings of later ages who do evil."
jj07.commentary: Kṣitigarbha answers the Buddha's request with tears. Repeating "Do not worry" three times, this is counted the most moving scene of the sutra: a promise to abandon no being.

jj08.heading: Merely Hearing the Name
jj08.plain: In future ages, if good men or good women hear the name of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva and join their palms, praise him, bow to him or long for him, they will pass beyond the wrongs of thirty kalpas.
jj08.commentary: From chapter six, where the Buddha praises Kṣitigarbha's merit. A small act of joining one's palms on hearing the name carries one beyond long ages of karma. It is the basis for repeatedly calling "Namo Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva" in Kṣitigarbha prayer.

jj09.heading: Do Not Kill on the Day of Death
jj09.plain: "So now, before the World-Honored One, the gods, dragons, the eight kinds of beings and the non-humans, I urge the beings of this world: on the day someone's life ends, please do not kill living things or create bad conditions, and do not sacrifice to ghosts or pray to goblins. Why? Such killing and sacrifice does not benefit the departed in the slightest; it only ties them to the causes of wrongdoing and makes them deeper and heavier."
jj09.commentary: Kṣitigarbha's words from chapter seven. It warns against the custom of slaughtering animals for funeral feasts or praying to spirits. If you would help the departed, do not harm life; make good merit instead.

jj10.heading: The Merit of the Forty-Nine Days
jj10.plain: "If within seven sevens (forty-nine days) after a death many good deeds are done for the departed, that being will leave the evil paths forever and be born among humans or gods to enjoy excellent happiness, and the living family will also gain measureless benefit. … If a man or woman did not cultivate good while alive and did much wrong, then even if after their death their family makes merit and does holy deeds for them, the departed gains only one part in seven of that merit, and the other six parts return to the living themselves."
jj10.commentary: This is the basis of the forty-nine-day ceremony. Merit made for the departed is not in vain, but most of it returns to the living who make it. So it is also a teaching that the most important thing is to cultivate good oneself while alive.

jj11.heading: Kṣitigarbha, Kṣitigarbha
jj11.plain: Then the World-Honored One raised his golden arm and again stroked the crown of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva's head, saying: "Kṣitigarbha, Kṣitigarbha. Your spiritual power is inconceivable, your compassion is inconceivable, your wisdom is inconceivable, your eloquence is inconceivable. Even if all the Buddhas of the ten directions praised your inconceivable deeds, they could not finish in a thousand million kalpas."
jj11.commentary: In the last chapter, the Buddha strokes Kṣitigarbha's head and entrusts beings to him. Deep trust and a heartfelt request sound in the voice that calls his name twice.

jj12.heading: Mantra for Removing Fixed Karma
jj12.meaning: Oṃ, you who hold the jewel, svāhā (mantras are chanted for their sound, not translated)
jj12.commentary: This mantra is chanted at the end of reciting Kṣitigarbha's name in prayer and memorial ceremonies. It carries Kṣitigarbha's great vow to melt even heavy karma whose results are fixed.
jj12.plain: Kṣitigarbha’s mantra, said to remove even fixed karma. It is chanted for its sound rather than translated.

trayastrimsa.definition: A heaven said to be on the summit of Mount Sumeru; the name means "thirty-three gods." The Buddha's mother, Queen Māyā, is said to have been born there after her death.

five-turbidities.definition: A world defiled by five kinds of murkiness: of the age, of views, of afflictions, of beings and of lifespans.

ksitigarbha.definition: "Earth Store" bodhisattva, who vowed to save beings of the six realms, the hells included, from Śākyamuni's passing until Maitreya comes. He is shown as a monk with shaven head holding a staff and a jewel.

six-paths.definition: The six worlds beings cycle through by karma: hells, hungry ghosts, animals, asuras, humans and heavenly beings.

nayuta.definition: An ancient Indian unit for a very large number.

kalpa.definition: An immeasurably long span of time.

avici.definition: The deepest and gravest hell, where suffering continues without interruption.

three-jewels.definition: The three treasures of Buddhism: the Buddha, the Dharma (teaching) and the Sangha (community of practitioners).

saha.definition: "The world of endurance": this world of ours, where we live bearing suffering.

maitreya.definition: The Buddha who will come to this world in the far future after Śākyamuni. He is said to dwell now as a bodhisattva in the Tuṣita Heaven.

nirvana.definition: The stillness in which the fires of greed, anger and delusion have gone out; the complete ending of suffering.

jambudvipa.definition: The continent said to lie south of Mount Sumeru: the world where humans live.

seven-sevens.definition: The forty-nine days after death before the next birth. Ceremonies are held every seventh day, and the one on the seventh seventh day is the forty-nine-day ceremony.

mantra.definition: The true words of Buddhas and bodhisattvas, chanted in their original sound rather than translated.
